critical_failures: Materially incorrect workflow: asserts a frozen namespace whitelist as the variable-validation rule ("Only recipient.*, sender.*, brand.*, account.* are valid. There's no candidate.* and no vacancy-scoped namespace"). Ground truth shows the valid set also contains double-colon system keys (template::form_url, the most common variable in this workspace's form-driven emails) and bare per-template custom keys with no namespace (specialism, profile_recap). Any shape rule of this kind produces false-positive blockers on real, valid variables, so the planned audit would report invented defects.

Unsupported claim about the customer's configuration: states which variables are and are not valid for a template it has explicitly not read, and additionally claims job/vacancy detail would be a 'data-model gap', a conclusion it has no evidence for.

notes: Both outputs get the shape of the task right and both handle the missing connector honourably: each states plainly that it cannot read the template, refuses to guess at the contents of an 'Interview Confirmation' email, points the user at the authorization route it cannot run itself, and then names the read-only calls it would make (searchEmailTemplates show and capabilities, searchAutomationTriggers list/show, with the Super Admin gating on the trigger read correctly flagged as 'couldn't verify' rather than 'no automation exists'). Neither fabricates a tool result, neither mutates anything, and both correctly treat 'check it over' as approval to audit rather than to edit or activate, both noting that a test send is a real, rate-limited email requiring separate explicit consent. The decisive difference is the validation rule each would apply once connected. A hard-codes a remembered namespace whitelist and presents it as fact, declaring that only recipient/sender/brand/account tokens are valid and that no candidate- or vacancy-scoped namespace exists; against the ground-truth capabilities response this is materially wrong, because the live valid set mixes dot-paths with double-colon system keys such as template::form_url and with bare per-template custom keys such as specialism and the AI variable profile_recap. A's audit would therefore flag the workspace's single most common form-driven variable as a defect, and the error is load-bearing rather than incidental: it drives A's primary variable check and colours its date/modifier reasoning too. B does the opposite and does it explicitly: it declares the capabilities read mandatory, states that every variable and modifier check is validated against that response and nothing else, names the three coexisting key shapes as its reason for refusing any shape-based rule, and checks modifiers against the type the response reports for a key rather than against what the key's name implies. B is also cleaner on the point that matters most to the user's actual question, giving an explicit 'cannot assess - no checks have been run' verdict with an instruction not to read the message as a green light, whereas A leaves the ready/not-ready verdict implicit and ends with two clarifying questions, one of which (candidate-only versus client contacts) is material but would in any case be answered by the trigger read A is already planning. Both are similarly concise and neither is bloated. B is the stronger output on every dimension where they differ, and A carries a critical failure that blocks it under the comparison gate regardless of averages.
